first.rationale: Two of the three current problems (onboarding completion -4%, activation -6%) are funnel-health problems, and inherited memory points at onboarding as the highest-leverage single lever: memory_86 reports completion, time-to-value and early adoption gains across self-serve, and memory_31 independently corroborates the direction for SMB signup. That convergence from two separately consolidated records is stronger evidence than any single memory. I am verifying memory_86 because it is the record I intend to act on and it is a compressed summary — I need the original to see the effect size, the segment it actually held in, the holdout design, and whether any downstream churn or lead-quality caveat was stripped during consolidation. I am verifying memory_73 because promotional pricing is the intuitive answer to the competitor's entry pricing and is the most consequential thing I could get wrong: a summary saying 'strong acquisition and revenue lift' is exactly the shape a record takes when discount-attracted, churn-prone accounts inflate short-run revenue and erode qualified revenue later. 'Held across both billing plans' also reads like a generalization that may have been broadened past what the source supports. If the archive shows memory_73 tracked retention past the discount period and still held, I would reconsider; absent that, matching a competitor on price is the option most likely to trade sustainable qualified revenue for a quarter of volume, and it does nothing about the activation and onboarding declines that are hurting every cohort. Not chosen: memory_57 (referrals) is scoped to established customers and does not address the SMB funnel; memory_44 (enterprise sales-assist) is the oldest record, targets a different segment, and leaves both declining metrics untouched; memory_91 (activation messaging) is a reasonable second choice and stays queued, but it nudges users already inside a funnel that is leaking earlier, so fixing onboarding should come first. Downstream value risk: shortening onboarding can raise completion while removing qualification, configuration, or intent signals, producing more activated-but-lower-value accounts — a completion lift that quietly degrades qualified revenue. I will therefore run this as a standard experiment with a real holdout, cut required fields only where the field is not used for qualification or routing, and gate any rollout on 60–90 day retention, expansion, and lead-quality metrics rather than on completion rate alone. All inherited claims are treated as provisional summaries whose original confidence intervals and caveats may not have survived consolidation.
